query: High-entropy alloys are valued for combining strength and ductility. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their dynamic mechanical behavior, and what controlled comparison would reveal it? State the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys, the dynamic mechanical behavior is governed by grain boundary–mediated nucleation of partial dislocations under rapid loading. This dislocation nucleation, enhanced by local chemical heterogeneities at the GBs, causes an earlier onset of plasticity and a higher initial work‐hardening rate compared to single‐crystal counterparts.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic (or near‐equiatomic) high‐entropy alloy (e.g., Cantor alloy) in a well‐characterized, polycrystalline state with controlled grain size.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA samples to controlled dynamic loading through varying strain rate tests while maintaining identical ambient temperature and environmental conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing should be performed over a range of strain rates (from moderate to high) at a temperature where thermal recovery mechanisms are not dominant. A controlled comparison between polycrystalline (with explicit grain boundaries) and single-crystal HEA samples is required.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that serve as preferential nucleation sites for partial dislocations, leading to the formation of stacking faults.
generation.mechanism: Under dynamic (high strain rate) loading, the heterogeneous chemistry and microstructural complexity at grain boundaries lower the energy barrier for the nucleation of partial dislocations. This results in an early accumulation of stacking faults which promotes work hardening and helps balance strength with ductility. In contrast, single-crystal HEAs, lacking such GB heterogeneities, require higher strains to nucleate dislocations and exhibit delayed work-hardening behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Polycrystalline HEA samples will exhibit a lower yield strain and a steeper initial work-hardening rate under high strain rate conditions relative to single crystals. Microstructural analysis should reveal an increased density of stacking faults and early partial dislocation nucleation at grain boundaries in the dynamically loaded polycrystalline samples.
generation.baseline: The dynamic mechanical response of single-crystal HEA samples tested under the same conditions, which are expected to show a higher threshold for dislocation nucleation and a more gradual work-hardening response.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected for equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEAs under conditions where dynamic effects dominate over thermal recovery (i.e., moderate to high strain rates and ambient or moderately elevated temperatures). The hypothesis may not hold if the microstructure is significantly altered (e.g., extreme grain refinement or annealing processes that modify GB chemistry) or under temperatures that promote extensive dynamic recovery.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of GB-mediated dislocation nucleation is supported by several observations, the precise quantitative contribution of local chemical heterogeneities versus lattice distortions and other factors (such as dynamic recovery) remains uncertain. Variability in grain size distribution and local composition may also influence the observed magnitude of effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one polycrystalline with controlled grain size and one single-crystal, both with equivalent composition and initial microstructural states. Subject all samples to identical dynamic loading tests across a range of strain rates while maintaining constant temperature. Utilize in situ high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM) to monitor dislocation nucleation events, stacking fault formation, and overall strain-hardening responses.
measurements: Work-hardening rate (initial slope of the stress-strain curve)
Density and spatial distribution of partial dislocations and stacking faults (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the polycrystalline samples do not exhibit a significantly lower yield strain and a steeper initial work-hardening rate relative to single crystals, or if both sample types show similar dislocation nucleation patterns and stacking fault densities under varying strain rates, then the hypothesis that grain boundary-mediated dislocation nucleation governs the distinctive dynamic mechanical behavior in HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Typical stress-strain curves of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA with different grain sizes deformed in compression at room temperature and 77 K (liquid-nitrogen temperature) are shown in Fig. 1. In all specimens, yielding and subsequent flow occurs smoothly without any discontinuities such as yield drops or serrated flow. At room temperature, the yield stress, defined here as the 0.2% offset stress increases with decreasing grain size, following conventional Hall-Petch behavior. The work-hardening rate also increases with decreasing grain size. A significant increase in yield stress occurs when the temperature is decreased to 77 K at a given grain size. For example, for 340 μm grain size, the yield stress at liquid-nitrogen temperature (260 MPa) is slightly more than twice that at room temperature (127 MPa).

We also observed similar LCO-induced strengthening effects for extended edge dislocations, using MD simulations at 300 K under a constant strain rate, see Supplementary Note 7 and Supplementary Figs. 16–18. The shear stress required to drive forward a leading partial dislocation needs to increase by as much as a factor of three, when an RSS has been annealed at 650 K to increase LCO. Also see Supplementary Movies 1–2 for the dynamic motion processes with dislocations evolving into rugged morphologies, detrapping from the nanoscale LCO heterogeneities. Note that the observed strengthening effect is not due to the lattice distortions caused by atomic size mismatch, as our MD/MC aging at Ta alleviates the effects of atomic size mismatch through rearranging unfavorable local atomic environments. While the Cantor alloy has been the subject of numerous studies in recent years, most of these have been mainly focused on the effects of element compositions away from the equiatomic one, stacking fault energies,, and lattice distortions. The role of GBs in the mechanical deformation of HEA alloys remains poorly understood. Tensile stress-strain diagrams for Cantor alloy bicrystals with [110] and [111] loading axes show that GBs facilitate the nucleation of partial dislocations, which with further deformation grow in the bulk crystal leaving behind stacking faults. This is in agreement with recent experimental findings demonstrating that GBs act as nucleation sites for mechanical nanotwins,. The bicrystals with a [111] loading axis were found to require more mechanical energy to nucleate dislocations from GBs compared to systems with a [110] loading axis. As shown in Figs. 5 and 6, nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ dislocations in the bicrystal systems occurred at lower strain values compared to their single crystal counterparts.
